topics.title: Harshavardhana and the kingdom of Kanauj
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Harshavardhana and the kingdom of Kanauj.
Use evidence or an example to apply Harshavardhana and the kingdom of Kanauj.
topics.explanation: Harshavardhana ruled a large north Indian kingdom in the seventh century CE. He inherited responsibility at Thanesar and later ruled from Kanauj, using alliances, administration and public works to strengthen his state. His expansion southward was checked near the Narmada by Pulakeshin II.
examples: Kanauj became an important political centre under Harshavardhana.
Harsha supported rest houses, learning centres and religious assemblies as public activities.
exercises: Why did Kanauj become important during Harshavardhana's reign?
Which ruler stopped Harshavardhana's expansion towards the Deccan?
solutions: It became the centre of Harshavardhana's large north Indian kingdom and an important seat of political power.
Pulakeshin II of the Chalukya dynasty stopped Harshavardhana near the Narmada.
practice_questions: Give one example of public welfare associated with Harshavardhana.
Why are alliances important when studying Harshavardhana's expansion?
practice_solutions: He supported works such as rest houses, wells, learning centres and religious assemblies; any one is acceptable.
Alliances helped rulers combine political and military support against rivals and extend their influence.

topics.title: Pulakeshin II and the Chalukyas of Vatapi
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Pulakeshin II and the Chalukyas of Vatapi.
Use evidence or an example to apply Pulakeshin II and the Chalukyas of Vatapi.
topics.explanation: The Chalukyas ruled a major Deccan state from Vatapi, now called Badami. Pulakeshin II expanded his influence across much of the Deccan and resisted Harshavardhana near the Narmada. His reign also supported architecture, painting and contacts recorded by travellers.
examples: Vatapi served as the Chalukya capital in the Deccan.
The Narmada region marked the meeting point of Harsha's and Pulakeshin II's political ambitions.
exercises: What was the capital of the Chalukyas discussed with Pulakeshin II?
Why is the Narmada important in the account of Harsha and Pulakeshin II?
solutions: Their capital was Vatapi, the place now known as Badami in Karnataka.
Pulakeshin II checked Harsha's southward expansion near the Narmada, making it an important political boundary.
practice_questions: Name one cultural achievement linked with the Chalukya period.
How did Pulakeshin II strengthen the Chalukya state?
practice_solutions: Rock-cut caves, temples, sculpture and painting developed during the period; any one suitable example is acceptable.
He expanded territory, defended the Deccan and maintained an influential capital and administration.

topics.title: Travellers, Nalanda and historical evidence
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Travellers, Nalanda and historical evidence.
Use evidence or an example to apply Travellers, Nalanda and historical evidence.
topics.explanation: Historians compare inscriptions, coins, buildings and written accounts to understand early medieval states. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, also written Hiuen Tsang, visited India during Harsha's time and studied at Nalanda. Such accounts are valuable evidence but should be compared with other sources because every observer writes from a particular viewpoint.
examples: Xuanzang's travel account describes aspects of society, learning and government in seventh-century India.
Coins and inscriptions can confirm names, titles, dates and political claims found in written accounts.
exercises: Why is Xuanzang's account useful to historians?
Why should a travel account be compared with inscriptions or coins?
solutions: It provides an eyewitness description of places, learning, society and political conditions during his travels in India.
Comparison can confirm details and reduce the risk of relying on one observer's limited viewpoint.
practice_questions: What made Nalanda an important learning centre?
Name two kinds of evidence used to study early medieval kingdoms.
practice_solutions: It attracted teachers and students, maintained a large collection of texts and supported advanced study in several fields.
Written accounts, inscriptions, coins, monuments and archaeological remains are examples; any two are acceptable.

topics.title: Rotation, day and night
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Rotation, day and night.
Use evidence or an example to apply Rotation, day and night.
topics.explanation: Earth rotates from west to east around an imaginary axis through the poles. One rotation takes about 24 hours and produces the daily pattern of day and night as different parts face the Sun. The boundary between the illuminated and dark halves is called the circle of illumination.
examples: India turns into sunlight and later away from it as Earth rotates.
A globe lit by a fixed lamp models day on the bright half and night on the dark half.
exercises: About how long does Earth take to complete one rotation?
Why do day and night occur?
solutions: Earth takes about 24 hours to complete one rotation.
Earth's rotation brings each place alternately into the sunlit half and the dark half.
practice_questions: In which general direction does Earth rotate?
What is the circle of illumination?
practice_solutions: Earth rotates from west to east.
It is the boundary separating Earth's sunlit half from its dark half.

topics.title: Revolution, axial tilt and seasons
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Revolution, axial tilt and seasons.
Use evidence or an example to apply Revolution, axial tilt and seasons.
topics.explanation: Earth revolves around the Sun in an elliptical orbit while its axis remains tilted by about 23.5 degrees. One revolution takes about 365¼ days. The combination of revolution and axial tilt changes the angle and duration of sunlight during the year, producing opposite seasons in the northern and southern hemispheres.
examples: When the Northern Hemisphere tilts more toward the Sun, it receives longer days and more direct sunlight.
Australia experiences winter during much of the period when India experiences summer.
exercises: About how long does Earth take to complete one revolution around the Sun?
Why are seasons opposite in the northern and southern hemispheres?
solutions: Earth takes about 365¼ days, which is approximately one year.
When one hemisphere tilts toward the Sun and receives more direct sunlight, the other tilts away and receives less.
practice_questions: Is Earth's orbit a perfect circle?
What two Earth movements and conditions work together to produce seasons?
practice_solutions: No. Earth's orbit is slightly elliptical, or oval-shaped.
Earth's revolution around the Sun and the tilt of its axis work together to produce seasons.

topics.title: Sunlight, shadows and local time
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Sunlight, shadows and local time.
Use evidence or an example to apply Sunlight, shadows and local time.
topics.explanation: Earth's rotation makes the Sun appear to move across the sky, so a vertical object's shadow changes direction and length through the day. Local solar time differs with longitude because places turn toward the Sun at different moments. Standard time gives a country or region one agreed clock time for coordination.
examples: A pole usually casts a long shadow in the morning and a shorter one near midday.
Two cities far apart in longitude can have different local solar times even when their clocks use one standard time.
exercises: Why is a noon shadow usually shorter than a morning shadow?
Why does local solar time differ from one longitude to another?
solutions: Near noon the Sun is higher in the sky, so its rays strike more steeply and form a shorter shadow.
Different longitudes face the Sun at different moments as Earth rotates.
practice_questions: Does every longitude have the same local solar time?
Why do countries adopt a standard time?
practice_solutions: No. Local solar time changes with longitude because Earth rotates.
A standard time gives people one agreed clock time for travel, communication, administration and daily activities.

topics.title: Purpose and functions of government
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Purpose and functions of government.
Use evidence or an example to apply Purpose and functions of government.
topics.explanation: Government makes and implements laws, maintains public order, protects rights and provides shared services. It also plans responses to economic, social and environmental problems. In a democracy, public authority is limited by the Constitution and must be used for the welfare of all people.
examples: A government builds and maintains public roads that many citizens use.
Disaster-response agencies coordinate rescue, relief and rehabilitation after a flood.
exercises: Name two basic functions of a government.
Why is government needed for public services?
solutions: Making and implementing laws, maintaining order, protecting rights and providing public services are examples; any two are acceptable.
Many services such as roads, schools and sanitation require common planning, funding and rules across a large population.
practice_questions: How does a Constitution limit government?
Give one government response to a natural disaster.
practice_solutions: It defines powers, institutions, procedures and protected rights that government must respect.
It may organize warnings, evacuation, rescue, relief supplies, medical help or rebuilding; any one is acceptable.

topics.title: Levels and organs of government
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Levels and organs of government.
Use evidence or an example to apply Levels and organs of government.
topics.explanation: India has local, state and Union levels of government, each with assigned responsibilities. The legislature makes laws, the executive implements laws and policies, and the judiciary interprets laws and settles disputes. These divisions help distribute work and create checks on public power.
examples: A municipal body manages many local services, while a state government manages subjects across the state.
A legislature debates a bill before it can become law through the required process.
exercises: Which organ of government primarily makes laws?
What is the main role of the executive?
solutions: The legislature primarily makes laws.
The executive implements laws, administers programmes and carries out public policy.
practice_questions: Why are there different levels of government?
What role does the judiciary perform?
practice_solutions: Different levels handle local, state-wide and national matters at the scale where they can be managed effectively.
It interprets laws, resolves disputes and protects legality and rights through court decisions.

topics.title: Democracy, elections and accountability
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Democracy, elections and accountability.
Use evidence or an example to apply Democracy, elections and accountability.
topics.explanation: Democracy gives citizens a role in choosing representatives and questioning public decisions. Regular elections, open debate, access to information and lawful criticism help make representatives accountable. Citizens also participate through community meetings, petitions and peaceful civic action.
examples: Voters compare candidates and policies before choosing a representative.
Residents raise a sanitation problem at a lawful local public meeting.
exercises: How do elections support accountability?
Name one way a citizen can participate between elections.
solutions: Citizens can evaluate representatives and choose whether to return them to office.
A citizen can attend public meetings, submit petitions, seek information or raise issues peacefully through lawful channels.
practice_questions: Why is access to reliable information important in a democracy?
Does democracy mean that elected leaders can ignore the Constitution?
practice_solutions: People need evidence about policies and performance to form opinions and hold public authorities accountable.
No. Elected leaders remain bound by constitutional limits, laws and protected rights.

topics.title: Rajput kingdoms and regional power
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Rajput kingdoms and regional power.
Use evidence or an example to apply Rajput kingdoms and regional power.
topics.explanation: Between the eighth and twelfth centuries, several Rajput clans established regional kingdoms in northern and western India. Important dynasties included the Gurjara-Pratiharas, Chauhans, Paramaras and Solankis. Their power was often regional, and alliances and rivalries changed over time.
examples: The Chauhans developed centres of power in parts of Rajasthan and around Delhi-Ajmer.
The Solankis ruled important parts of Gujarat from Anahilapataka, or Patan.
exercises: Name two dynasties associated with the Rajput age.
Why is the Rajput age described as a period of regional kingdoms?
solutions: The Gurjara-Pratiharas, Chauhans, Paramaras and Solankis are examples; any two are acceptable.
Power was divided among several dynasties controlling different regions rather than one state ruling the entire area.
practice_questions: Which Rajput dynasty is strongly associated with medieval Gujarat?
How could alliances affect a regional kingdom?
practice_solutions: The Solanki, or Chaulukya, dynasty is strongly associated with medieval Gujarat.
Alliances could provide military or political support, while broken alliances could leave a kingdom more vulnerable.

topics.title: Rajput administration and society
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Rajput administration and society.
Use evidence or an example to apply Rajput administration and society.
topics.explanation: Rajput rulers depended on forts, local chiefs and land-based revenue to govern. Samantas or subordinate chiefs could provide troops and collect revenue, but strong local power could also weaken central control. Agriculture, crafts and trade supported towns, courts and temples.
examples: A local chief might collect revenue and supply soldiers to a regional ruler.
Fortified towns protected political centres and routes in times of conflict.
exercises: Who were samantas in many early medieval kingdoms?
Why could powerful local chiefs weaken a king?
solutions: They were subordinate chiefs or landholders who owed service, revenue or military support to a ruler.
They controlled local resources and troops and might resist orders or become independent when central power declined.
practice_questions: Name one economic activity that supported Rajput-era towns.
Why were forts important to regional rulers?
practice_solutions: Agriculture, craft production and regional trade supported towns; any one is acceptable.
Forts protected capitals, routes, supplies and people and served as centres of political control.

topics.title: Rajput culture, literature and architecture
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Rajput culture, literature and architecture.
Use evidence or an example to apply Rajput culture, literature and architecture.
topics.explanation: Rajput courts supported regional languages, poetry, sculpture, temples, forts, lakes and stepwells. Architecture combined practical needs with religious and artistic expression. These remains are historical evidence and shared heritage that should be studied and preserved.
examples: A stepwell stored water while also displaying skilled stone carving.
Temple inscriptions can record patrons, donations, dates and social activity.
exercises: Give two kinds of structures associated with Rajput patronage.
How can an inscription help a historian?
solutions: Temples, forts, lakes and stepwells are examples; any two are acceptable.
It can provide names, dates, donations, titles, events or information about institutions.
practice_questions: Why should medieval monuments be preserved?
How did court patronage support culture?
practice_solutions: They are evidence of history, architecture, technology and culture and form part of shared heritage.
Rulers and elites provided resources to writers, artists, builders and religious or learning institutions.

topics.title: Latitude, longitude and coordinates
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Latitude, longitude and coordinates.
Use evidence or an example to apply Latitude, longitude and coordinates.
topics.explanation: Latitude measures angular distance north or south of the Equator, while longitude measures angular distance east or west of the Prime Meridian. Together they form a coordinate system for locating places on Earth. Parallels of latitude do not meet, while meridians meet at the poles.
examples: A location at 20 degrees north lies north of the Equator.
A map grid can identify a place by stating its latitude first and longitude second.
exercises: What does latitude measure?
What does longitude measure?
solutions: Latitude measures angular distance north or south of the Equator.
Longitude measures angular distance east or west of the Prime Meridian.
practice_questions: Why are both latitude and longitude needed to locate a place precisely?
Where do meridians of longitude meet?
practice_solutions: Latitude fixes its north-south position and longitude fixes its east-west position, giving one coordinate intersection.
They meet at the North Pole and the South Pole.

topics.title: Longitude, local time and standard time
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Longitude, local time and standard time.
Use evidence or an example to apply Longitude, local time and standard time.
topics.explanation: Earth completes 360 degrees of rotation in about 24 hours, so it turns roughly 15 degrees per hour. Places eastward generally experience local noon earlier than places westward. India uses Indian Standard Time based on the standard meridian of 82.5 degrees east to coordinate clocks across the country.
examples: A place 15 degrees farther east has local solar time about one hour ahead.
IST lets trains and offices use one clock time across India despite differences in local solar time.
exercises: How many degrees does Earth rotate in about one hour?
What longitude is used as the standard meridian for Indian Standard Time?
solutions: Earth rotates about 15 degrees in one hour.
Indian Standard Time is based on 82.5 degrees east longitude.
practice_questions: Which place generally has earlier local time, one farther east or one farther west?
Why does India use one standard time?
practice_solutions: The place farther east generally has earlier local solar time.
One standard time avoids confusion and coordinates transport, communication, administration and daily schedules.

topics.title: Map location and directional reasoning
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Map location and directional reasoning.
Use evidence or an example to apply Map location and directional reasoning.
topics.explanation: Maps use direction, scale, symbols and coordinate grids to describe relative and absolute location. The Equator divides northern and southern hemispheres, and the Prime Meridian helps divide eastern and western hemispheres. A good location statement identifies both position and a clear reference system.
examples: India lies north of the Equator and east of the Prime Meridian.
A map scale converts a measured map distance into an estimated ground distance.
exercises: In which two hemispheres is India mainly located?
What does a map scale show?
solutions: India is in the Northern Hemisphere and the Eastern Hemisphere.
It shows the relationship between distance on the map and corresponding distance on the ground.
practice_questions: Why must map symbols be explained in a legend?
Distinguish absolute location from relative location.
practice_solutions: A legend tells the reader what each symbol or colour represents.
Absolute location uses coordinates, while relative location describes a place in relation to another place or feature.

chapters.title: Semester 1 — Administrative System and Architecture During the Medieval Age

topics.title: Delhi Sultanate administration
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Delhi Sultanate administration.
Use evidence or an example to apply Delhi Sultanate administration.
topics.explanation: Delhi Sultanate rulers governed through the Sultan, ministers, military officers, provincial authorities and local officials. Revenue assignments called iqtas supported administration and troops, though arrangements changed under different rulers. Effective control depended on communication, revenue collection and supervision of powerful officials.
examples: An iqta-holder collected assigned revenue and maintained responsibilities for the state.
Provincial officials connected the central court with districts and local communities.
exercises: What was an iqta in the Delhi Sultanate system?
Why did the Sultan need provincial and local officials?
solutions: It was an assigned revenue area whose income supported an official's administrative or military responsibilities.
A large territory could not be governed directly from Delhi, so officials carried out revenue, order and administration in different regions.
practice_questions: Name one factor needed for effective medieval administration.
Why could an overly powerful provincial governor challenge the centre?
practice_solutions: Reliable revenue, communication, records, military organization and supervision were important; any one is acceptable.
Control of local revenue and troops could allow a governor to resist central authority or seek independence.

topics.title: Medieval towns, trade and society
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Medieval towns, trade and society.
Use evidence or an example to apply Medieval towns, trade and society.
topics.explanation: Medieval towns grew around capitals, forts, ports, temples and markets. Farmers, artisans, merchants, officials and religious communities were linked through taxes, production and exchange. Inland routes and ports connected Indian regions with wider commercial networks.
examples: A port town connected inland cotton producers with merchants using sea routes.
A capital attracted officials, soldiers, builders, traders and service workers.
exercises: Name two places around which medieval towns often developed.
How did trade routes help a town grow?
solutions: Capitals, forts, ports, temples and markets are examples; any two are acceptable.
They brought merchants, goods, transport work, taxes and demand for local services and crafts.
practice_questions: Why were artisans important to medieval cities?
How were villages and towns economically connected?
practice_solutions: They produced textiles, metalwork, building materials and other goods needed by residents, courts and traders.
Villages supplied food and raw materials, while towns provided markets, services and manufactured goods.

topics.title: Sultanate architecture and building methods
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Sultanate architecture and building methods.
Use evidence or an example to apply Sultanate architecture and building methods.
topics.explanation: Sultanate architecture used arches, domes, minarets, courtyards, carved stone and geometric or calligraphic decoration. Builders combined ideas arriving through new ruling traditions with skilled Indian materials and craftsmanship. Buildings reveal technology, patronage and cultural interaction, not just the names of rulers.
examples: An arch transfers weight toward its supports and can span an opening.
A mosque courtyard and minaret show both functional planning and architectural style.
exercises: Name two common features of Sultanate architecture.
Why does medieval architecture show cultural interaction?
solutions: Arches, domes, minarets, courtyards and geometric or calligraphic decoration are examples; any two are acceptable.
Design traditions from different regions were adapted by Indian builders using local skills, materials and artistic forms.
practice_questions: What can a building reveal besides the ruler who commissioned it?
Why is an arch useful in construction?
practice_solutions: It can reveal technology, labour, materials, artistic taste, religious use and social priorities.
It spans an opening and directs the load toward supporting sides or pillars.

chapters.title: Semester 1 — India: Location, Border, Area and Physiography

topics.title: India's location, extent and neighbours
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of India's location, extent and neighbours.
Use evidence or an example to apply India's location, extent and neighbours.
topics.explanation: India lies in South Asia, mainly in the Northern and Eastern hemispheres. The Himalayas form a major northern boundary, while the Arabian Sea, Bay of Bengal and Indian Ocean surround the peninsula. India's land and maritime position links South Asia with routes toward West Asia, Africa and Southeast Asia.
examples: The Arabian Sea lies west of India and the Bay of Bengal lies east.
India shares land boundaries with several South Asian countries and sea routes with the wider Indian Ocean region.
exercises: In which part of Asia is India located?
Name the water body west of India and the one east of India.
solutions: India is located in South Asia.
The Arabian Sea is to the west and the Bay of Bengal is to the east.
practice_questions: How does India's location support overseas connections?
Which major mountain system forms a natural boundary in the north?
practice_solutions: Its long coastline and central position in the northern Indian Ocean connect sea routes toward Africa, West Asia and Southeast Asia.
The Himalayas form the major northern mountain boundary.

topics.title: Major physiographic divisions of India
aliases: Himalayas plains plateau desert coast islands
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Major physiographic divisions of India.
Use evidence or an example to apply Major physiographic divisions of India.
topics.explanation: India's major physiographic divisions include the Himalayan Mountains, Northern Plains, Peninsular Plateau, Indian Desert, Coastal Plains and Islands. Each division differs in relief, rocks, soils, water and human use. These landforms influence settlement, farming, transport and natural hazards.
examples: The Northern Plains contain extensive alluvial deposits brought by river systems.
The Peninsular Plateau contains old rocks and important mineral regions.
exercises: Name four major physiographic divisions of India.
Why are the Northern Plains important for agriculture?
solutions: The Himalayas, Northern Plains, Peninsular Plateau, Indian Desert, Coastal Plains and Islands are the main divisions; any four are acceptable.
River-deposited alluvial soils, level land and water availability support extensive farming.
practice_questions: How can mountain relief affect transport?
Which division contains many of India's old rocks and mineral areas?
practice_solutions: Steep slopes and high passes make routes more difficult and concentrate transport in valleys and passes.
The Peninsular Plateau contains many old rocks and major mineral regions.

topics.title: Relief, rivers and human activity
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Relief, rivers and human activity.
Use evidence or an example to apply Relief, rivers and human activity.
topics.explanation: Relief affects climate, drainage, soils, vegetation and where people build settlements. Rivers provide water, fertile sediment, transport possibilities and energy, but floods can also create risk. Responsible planning matches land use with local physical conditions instead of treating every region alike.
examples: Dense settlement often develops on accessible plains with water and fertile soil.
Building carelessly on a floodplain can increase damage during high river flow.
exercises: Give two ways rivers support human activity.
Why can floodplains be both useful and risky?
solutions: Rivers provide water, fertile soil, irrigation, transport, fisheries and energy; any two are acceptable.
They often have fertile soil and water access, but they can be inundated during floods.
practice_questions: How does relief influence settlement patterns?
Why should land-use planning consider physical geography?
practice_solutions: Level, accessible land usually supports denser settlement, while steep or difficult terrain often supports more scattered settlement.
It helps match farming, buildings and transport with local slopes, water, soils and natural hazards.

chapters.title: Semester 1 — Delhi during the Medieval Period

topics.title: Founding dynasties of the Delhi Sultanate
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Founding dynasties of the Delhi Sultanate.
Use evidence or an example to apply Founding dynasties of the Delhi Sultanate.
topics.explanation: The Delhi Sultanate began in the early thirteenth century and was ruled successively by the Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi dynasties. Early rulers such as Qutbuddin Aibak and Iltutmish established institutions and control around Delhi. Razia is remembered as a woman who ruled despite strong political opposition.
examples: Iltutmish consolidated authority and strengthened Delhi as a political centre.
Razia's reign shows how court politics and gender expectations affected succession.
exercises: Name the five main dynasties of the Delhi Sultanate in order.
Why is Iltutmish important in the early Delhi Sultanate?
solutions: They were the Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi dynasties.
He consolidated the new state, strengthened Delhi and developed administrative institutions.
practice_questions: What challenge did Razia face as ruler?
Which dynasty ruled the Delhi Sultanate immediately before the Khaljis?
practice_solutions: She faced opposition from powerful nobles and social expectations that resisted a woman exercising sovereign authority.
The Mamluk, or Slave, dynasty ruled immediately before the Khaljis.

topics.title: Khalji and Tughlaq policies
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Khalji and Tughlaq policies.
Use evidence or an example to apply Khalji and Tughlaq policies.
topics.explanation: Alauddin Khalji expanded the Sultanate and used market controls and revenue measures to support a large army. Muhammad bin Tughlaq attempted ambitious policies such as transferring the capital and issuing token currency, but weak planning and enforcement caused serious problems. These cases show that policy goals and practical implementation must both be studied.
examples: Price controls helped Alauddin Khalji try to maintain a large army at controlled cost.
Token currency failed when counterfeit coins spread and trust in the system collapsed.
exercises: Why did Alauddin Khalji introduce market controls?
Why did Muhammad bin Tughlaq's token currency face difficulty?
solutions: He wanted to regulate prices and supplies so a large army could be maintained at manageable cost.
Counterfeiting and weak control reduced trust, so the tokens could not function reliably as money.
practice_questions: What lesson can be learned from the attempted capital transfer?
How should historians evaluate an ambitious policy?
practice_solutions: A major policy needs realistic planning for distance, people, resources and administration before implementation.
They should compare its goal, method, implementation, effects and evidence rather than judging only the ruler's intention.

topics.title: Delhi as a medieval political and cultural centre
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Delhi as a medieval political and cultural centre.
Use evidence or an example to apply Delhi as a medieval political and cultural centre.
topics.explanation: Delhi grew through a series of fortified settlements, courts, markets, water systems and religious buildings created by different dynasties. Its location connected routes across northern India. Surviving monuments and archaeological layers show both political change and continuity in urban life.
examples: The Qutb complex preserves structures from different phases of early Sultanate building.
Reservoirs and canals were essential infrastructure for a large inland city.
exercises: Why was Delhi well placed to become a major political centre?
What do Delhi's multiple fortified settlements indicate?
solutions: It connected important routes across northern India and could control access between regions.
They show that successive rulers expanded, shifted or rebuilt political centres over time.

Stepwells combined water storage with architecture suited to Gujarat's climate.

learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Climate controls, monsoon and seasons.
Use evidence or an example to apply Climate controls, monsoon and seasons.
topics.explanation: India's climate is influenced by latitude, altitude, relief, distance from the sea and seasonal winds. The monsoon brings much of the annual rainfall, but mountains and location make rainfall uneven. Long-term climate patterns shape crops, water availability, housing and daily life.
examples: The Western Ghats force moisture-laden winds upward, producing heavy rain on the windward side.
Coastal places usually have a smaller annual temperature range than places far inland.
exercises: Name three factors that influence India's climate.
Why do coastal places often have more moderate temperatures?
solutions: Latitude, altitude, relief, distance from the sea, winds and ocean conditions are factors; any three are acceptable.
The sea heats and cools slowly, reducing temperature extremes near the coast.
practice_questions: How can mountains affect rainfall?
Why is the monsoon important to India?
practice_solutions: Mountains force moist air to rise and cool, increasing rain on one side and sometimes creating a rain-shadow region on the other.
It supplies much of the rainfall needed for farming, water storage, rivers and ecosystems.

learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Water, soils and mineral resources.
Use evidence or an example to apply Water, soils and mineral resources.
topics.explanation: Water, soil and minerals support life and economic activity, but their distribution is uneven. Soil forms slowly and can lose fertility through erosion or misuse. Minerals are non-renewable on a human timescale, so efficient use, recycling and careful extraction are important.
examples: Contour planting can slow runoff and reduce soil erosion on a slope.
Recycling metal reduces the need to extract the same amount of new ore.

Useful mineral deposits form over geological time and cannot be replaced quickly after extraction.

It recovers usable material from products and reduces demand for fresh mining and processing.

A citizen may challenge an unlawful government action through the judicial process.

What does rule of law mean?
solutions: Courts resolve disputes, apply laws, protect rights and provide lawful remedies when rules are broken.
It means everyone, including government authorities, is subject to publicly known laws and legal procedures.
practice_questions: Why should judges be independent?
Why must both sides receive a fair hearing?
practice_solutions: They must decide according to law and evidence without improper political, financial or personal pressure.

Humayun's exile shows that winning a throne did not automatically secure lasting control.

Sher Shah Suri displaced Humayun from power for a period.

practice_solutions: It faced rival powers, contested succession, limited institutions and difficulty controlling a large territory.
Political control could be lost and regained as alliances, military strength and rival states changed.

topics.explanation: Crop choice depends on temperature, rainfall, soil, water, labour and market access. Kharif crops are generally sown with the monsoon, while rabi crops are generally sown in the cooler season. Irrigation and improved methods can reduce risk, but sustainable farming must protect soil and water.

practice_questions: Name three factors that influence crop choice.

practice_solutions: Temperature, rainfall, soil, irrigation, labour and market access are factors; any three are acceptable.

solutions: Bills, warranty documents, labels, photographs, messages and service records can support the complaint.

practice_questions: Why should a consumer first contact the seller or provider?
What does consumer redress mean?
practice_solutions: The seller may be able to verify and resolve the problem quickly before formal escalation is needed.
It means a remedy for a valid complaint, such as repair, replacement, refund, compensation or correction as allowed by applicable rules.

topics.title: Temple, fort and water architecture
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Temple, fort and water architecture.
Use evidence or an example to apply Temple, fort and water architecture.
topics.explanation: Medieval builders designed temples, forts, stepwells, tanks and gateways for religious, political and practical needs. Site, stone, climate and available skills shaped each structure. Carvings and inscriptions add cultural evidence, while walls, drainage and water systems reveal engineering choices.
examples: A hill fort uses elevation and strong gateways to control access.
A stepwell provides descending access to water as the water level changes.
exercises: Why were stepwells useful in regions with seasonal water levels?
Name two practical features of a fort.
solutions: Their descending steps allowed people to reach water at different depths through the year.
Defensive walls, controlled gateways, watch points, storage and water systems are examples; any two are acceptable.
practice_questions: How does building material affect architecture?
What can carvings reveal to historians?
practice_solutions: Local stone, brick, timber and mortar influence strength, carving, span, maintenance and appearance.
They can reveal beliefs, clothing, occupations, artistic styles, patrons and stories valued by society.

topics.title: Sultanate and Mughal architectural forms
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Sultanate and Mughal architectural forms.
Use evidence or an example to apply Sultanate and Mughal architectural forms.
topics.explanation: Sultanate and Mughal buildings often used arches, domes, minarets, large gateways, courtyards and geometric planning. Mughal design developed formal gardens, balanced layouts and refined stone or inlay work. Local craftsmen and regional traditions shaped how these forms appeared in different places.
examples: A charbagh divides a formal garden into planned sections using paths and water channels.
The Red Fort combines defensive walls with palaces and administrative spaces.
exercises: What is a charbagh?
Name three features common in Sultanate or Mughal architecture.
solutions: It is a formal garden divided into four main sections, usually organized with paths and water channels.
Arches, domes, minarets, gateways, courtyards, gardens and geometric decoration are examples; any three are acceptable.
practice_questions: Why did the same architectural tradition look different across regions?
How can a palace-fort serve more than one purpose?
practice_solutions: Builders adapted designs to local materials, climate, craftsmanship and earlier regional forms.
It can provide defense while also housing rulers, officials, ceremonies and administration.

topics.title: Gujarat monuments and heritage conservation
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Gujarat monuments and heritage conservation.
Use evidence or an example to apply Gujarat monuments and heritage conservation.
topics.explanation: Gujarat's medieval heritage includes temples, mosques, tombs, forts, stepwells, lakes and carved gateways. Structures such as the Sidi Saiyyed Mosque's stone screens show exceptional craftsmanship. Conservation requires documentation, careful repair, controlled use and protection from vandalism, pollution and unsuitable construction.
examples: A carved stone screen filters light while forming a detailed decorative pattern.
Repair using incompatible cement can trap moisture and damage historic stone.
exercises: What is the Sidi Saiyyed Mosque especially known for?
Name two threats to historic monuments.
solutions: It is especially known for its finely carved stone lattice screens, or jalis.
Vandalism, pollution, water damage, neglect, crowd pressure and unsuitable repair are threats; any two are acceptable.
practice_questions: Why should conservation begin with documentation?
Why must repair materials be compatible with an old structure?
practice_solutions: Records of condition, materials and earlier changes help experts plan repairs and monitor damage accurately.
Incompatible materials can change moisture movement, weight or chemical conditions and cause further damage.

topics.title: Regional languages, clothing and food
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Regional languages, clothing and food.
Use evidence or an example to apply Regional languages, clothing and food.
topics.explanation: India's social life varies with language, climate, crops, occupations, history and contact between communities. Clothing and food reflect both local conditions and cultural choice. Regional patterns are useful for study, but individuals should not be stereotyped because every region contains internal diversity.
examples: Rice-based dishes are common in many high-rainfall and coastal regions, but diets still vary within those regions.
Light cotton clothing is practical in hot conditions, while local traditions influence style and design.
exercises: Name three factors that influence regional food or clothing.
Why should regional descriptions not become stereotypes?
solutions: Climate, crops, occupations, history, trade, religion and cultural tradition are factors; any three are acceptable.
People within the same region have different identities, choices, occupations and family traditions.
practice_questions: How can climate influence clothing?
How does agriculture influence cuisine?
practice_solutions: Temperature, rainfall and humidity affect the materials and designs people find practical.
Locally grown grains, pulses, vegetables, oils and spices become common ingredients in regional food traditions.

topics.title: Festivals, arts and shared traditions
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Festivals, arts and shared traditions.
Use evidence or an example to apply Festivals, arts and shared traditions.
topics.explanation: Festivals, music, dance, theatre and crafts express community memory and creativity. Traditions change as people migrate, exchange ideas and use new materials or media. Many celebrations are shared across communities or have regional variations, showing both diversity and connection.
examples: A harvest festival may have different names and customs in different states while marking a similar seasonal event.
A folk dance can preserve local stories while adapting its performance for new audiences.
exercises: How can one festival show both unity and diversity?
Why do cultural traditions change over time?
solutions: People may share the same seasonal or cultural purpose while using different regional names, foods, music and rituals.
Migration, technology, trade, new audiences and contact among communities introduce new forms and meanings.
practice_questions: Name two forms of cultural expression.
How can a local art form support community identity?
practice_solutions: Music, dance, theatre, painting, storytelling, textiles and crafts are examples; any two are acceptable.
It carries shared stories, skills, symbols and memories across generations.

topics.title: Unity in diversity and respectful citizenship
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Unity in diversity and respectful citizenship.
Use evidence or an example to apply Unity in diversity and respectful citizenship.
topics.explanation: Unity in diversity means building common citizenship while respecting differences of language, region, religion and culture. The Constitution promises equality and rejects discrimination. Respectful citizenship involves listening, checking stereotypes and ensuring that public spaces and opportunities include everyone.
examples: Classmates explain different home languages without treating one language as superior.
A public event provides information in forms that more community members can understand.
exercises: What does unity in diversity mean?
Why are stereotypes harmful?
solutions: It means sharing equal citizenship and common institutions while respecting cultural, linguistic, regional and religious differences.
They replace evidence about individuals with oversimplified assumptions and can lead to unfair treatment.
practice_questions: Give one way a school can support inclusion.
Does respecting diversity require accepting discrimination as a tradition?
practice_solutions: It can use fair rules, accessible activities, respectful language and opportunities for different students to participate; any one is acceptable.
No. Cultural respect must remain consistent with equality, dignity and constitutional rights.

topics.title: Public property, private property and common use
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Public property, private property and common use.
Use evidence or an example to apply Public property, private property and common use.
topics.explanation: Private property is owned or lawfully controlled by a person or organization, while public property is provided or maintained for community use through public institutions. Schools, parks, roads and buses may be public facilities. Public access does not mean there are no rules; shared use requires lawful and responsible behaviour.
examples: A personal school bag is private property, while a municipal park is public property.
A public bus is shared infrastructure that users must not damage.
exercises: Distinguish public property from private property.
Give three examples of public property.
solutions: Public property is maintained for community or governmental use, while private property is owned or controlled by a particular person or organization.
Public roads, parks, schools, libraries, buses and government hospitals are examples; any three are acceptable.
practice_questions: Does public property mean anyone may use it in any way?
Why is a public library considered a shared facility?
practice_solutions: No. Its use is governed by laws and rules so it remains safe and available for everyone.
It is maintained for community access and its books, space and services are used by many people under common rules.

topics.title: Care, maintenance and civic responsibility
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Care, maintenance and civic responsibility.
Use evidence or an example to apply Care, maintenance and civic responsibility.
topics.explanation: Public property is funded and maintained from shared resources, so damage imposes costs on the whole community. Responsible users avoid littering, vandalism and waste, follow safety rules and report faults. Peaceful protest and lawful complaint never justify damaging shared facilities.
examples: Reporting a leaking public tap prevents water loss and repair costs from growing.
Writing on a monument damages evidence and enjoyment that belong to everyone.
exercises: Why does damage to public property affect everyone?
What should a student do after noticing a leaking school tap?
solutions: Repair uses shared funds and the damage can reduce or interrupt services used by the community.
The student should close it if safe and report the fault promptly to a responsible adult or maintenance authority.
practice_questions: Is damaging a bus an acceptable form of protest?
Give two responsible behaviours in a public park.
practice_solutions: No. It harms shared property, risks safety and breaks the law; concerns should be expressed peacefully through lawful methods.
Using bins, protecting plants, following rules, conserving water and reporting damage are examples; any two are acceptable.

topics.title: Community action and resource conservation
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Community action and resource conservation.
Use evidence or an example to apply Community action and resource conservation.
topics.explanation: Communities can improve shared facilities by identifying a problem, gathering evidence, contacting the responsible authority and following up. Conservation reduces waste of water, electricity and materials in public places. Constructive participation focuses on solutions rather than blame or unsafe confrontation.
examples: Students record when a tap leaks and submit the evidence to the school office for repair.
A neighbourhood group requests labelled waste bins and organizes an approved awareness activity.
exercises: List four steps in a constructive community action.
How can a school conserve electricity?
solutions: Identify the issue, gather evidence, contact the responsible authority and follow up on the response.
It can switch off unused lights and equipment, use efficient devices and monitor unnecessary use.
practice_questions: Why is evidence useful in a public-service complaint?
What is the safest response if someone is damaging public property?
practice_solutions: Dates, locations and photographs make the problem clear and help the authority verify and solve it.
Do not confront them dangerously; inform a responsible adult, staff member or appropriate authority and provide accurate details.

topics.title: Bhakti traditions and vernacular devotion
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Bhakti traditions and vernacular devotion.
Use evidence or an example to apply Bhakti traditions and vernacular devotion.
topics.explanation: Bhakti traditions emphasized personal devotion and expressed religious ideas through songs and poetry in regional languages. Earlier Alvar and Nayanar poet-saints in South India influenced later devotional movements. Bhakti teachers differed in belief and practice, so the movement should be understood as many related traditions rather than one uniform organization.
examples: A devotional poem in a regional language could reach people beyond a small learned elite.
Some Bhakti teachers emphasized loving devotion, while others criticized empty ritual or social exclusion.
exercises: Why were regional languages important to Bhakti traditions?
Who were the Alvars and Nayanars?
solutions: They allowed devotional ideas and songs to reach wider local audiences in familiar speech.
They were early South Indian poet-saints devoted mainly to Vishnu and Shiva respectively.
practice_questions: Why should Bhakti not be treated as one uniform movement?
Name one social message found in some Bhakti teachings.
practice_solutions: Different teachers followed different deities, philosophies, regions, languages and practices.
Some teachers emphasized human equality, dignity, devotion over status or criticism of social exclusion; any one is acceptable.

topics.title: Sufi traditions, teachers and communities
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Sufi traditions, teachers and communities.
Use evidence or an example to apply Sufi traditions, teachers and communities.
topics.explanation: Sufi traditions developed within Islam and emphasized disciplined spiritual practice, remembrance of God, ethical conduct and guidance from teachers. Khanqahs could serve as centres of teaching, hospitality and community contact. Different Sufi orders had distinct practices and relationships with rulers and society.
examples: A khanqah could welcome travellers and provide a place for teaching and service.
Poetry and music were used in some Sufi traditions, while other orders followed different devotional practices.
exercises: What was a khanqah?
Name two values emphasized in many Sufi traditions.
solutions: It was a Sufi centre or lodge used for spiritual teaching, community life, hospitality and service.
Devotion, remembrance of God, ethical conduct, humility, service and compassion are examples; any two are acceptable.
practice_questions: Did all Sufi orders follow exactly the same practices?
How could a Sufi centre connect with the wider community?
practice_solutions: No. Orders differed in discipline, teaching, devotional expression and relationships with political authority.
It could provide teaching, hospitality, charity, counselling and a shared place for visitors.

topics.title: Saint-poets, equality and cultural exchange
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Saint-poets, equality and cultural exchange.
Use evidence or an example to apply Saint-poets, equality and cultural exchange.
topics.explanation: Saint-poets such as Kabir, Guru Nanak, Narsinh Mehta, Mirabai and Tukaram used memorable language to express devotion and ethical teaching. Their messages were not identical, but many questioned pride, social exclusion or conflict based on identity. Their compositions influenced regional literature, music and shared cultural memory.
examples: Kabir's verses often challenge narrow labels and emphasize sincere spiritual understanding.
Narsinh Mehta's Gujarati devotional poetry links devotion with compassion and regard for others.
exercises: Name three saint-poets associated with medieval devotional traditions.
What broad social concern appears in many saint-poets' teachings?
solutions: Kabir, Guru Nanak, Narsinh Mehta, Mirabai, Tukaram and others are examples; any three are acceptable.
Many criticized pride, exclusion, discrimination or conflict and emphasized dignity, devotion and ethical conduct.
practice_questions: How did saint-poets influence regional culture?
Did Kabir, Guru Nanak and Mirabai teach exactly the same doctrine?
practice_solutions: Their poems and songs shaped languages, music, public memory and religious or ethical discussion.
No. They had distinct beliefs and contexts, though some of their teachings shared themes such as devotion and criticism of social barriers.

topics.title: North America: landforms, climate and economy
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of North America: landforms, climate and economy.
Use evidence or an example to apply North America: landforms, climate and economy.
topics.explanation: North America extends from the Arctic to tropical latitudes. Major features include western mountain systems, central plains, eastern highlands, large lakes and major river basins. Its varied climate and resources support farming, forestry, mining, manufacturing and service economies, while environmental impacts differ by region.
examples: The Rocky Mountains form a major western mountain system.
The Great Plains support extensive agriculture across parts of Canada and the United States.
exercises: Name three major physical features of North America.
Why does North America have varied climates?
solutions: The Rocky Mountains, Great Plains, Appalachian Highlands, Great Lakes and Mississippi-Missouri basin are examples; any three are acceptable.
It spans many latitudes and has major differences in altitude, relief, ocean influence and air movement.
practice_questions: How do the Great Plains support economic activity?
Name one environmental challenge linked with resource use in North America.
practice_solutions: Their broad land and suitable soils support large-scale farming, grazing, transport and settlement.
Habitat loss, water stress, pollution, soil degradation and high energy use are examples; any one is acceptable.

topics.title: South America: Andes, Amazon and regional diversity
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of South America: Andes, Amazon and regional diversity.
Use evidence or an example to apply South America: Andes, Amazon and regional diversity.
topics.explanation: South America's major features include the Andes along the west, the Amazon basin, eastern highlands and southern plains. Equatorial, tropical, highland, desert and temperate climates occur across the continent. Farming, mining, forestry, industry and services support economies, while conservation of forests and water is a major concern.
examples: The Andes influence settlement, transport, climate and river systems along western South America.
The Amazon basin contains an immense river network and tropical forest ecosystem.
exercises: Where are the Andes located within South America?
Why is the Amazon basin globally important?
solutions: The Andes extend along the western side of South America.
It contains vast tropical forests, biodiversity, freshwater systems and major carbon and climate relationships.
practice_questions: Name two contrasting climate regions in South America.
Why can deforestation in the Amazon affect more than the cleared site?
practice_solutions: Equatorial rainforest, highland, desert, tropical grassland and temperate regions are examples; any two are acceptable.
It can alter habitats, carbon storage, water cycling, soil protection and downstream river conditions.

topics.title: Europe: peninsulas, rivers and human development
learning_objectives: Explain the main ideas of Europe: peninsulas, rivers and human development.
Use evidence or an example to apply Europe: peninsulas, rivers and human development.
topics.explanation: Europe has an irregular coastline, many peninsulas, navigable rivers, plains and mountain systems such as the Alps. Its temperate location, waterways, resources and dense transport links supported urbanization and industrial development. Europe contains many countries and languages, so geographic patterns should not be mistaken for cultural uniformity.
examples: The Rhine links inland industrial and urban regions with the North Sea.
The Alps affect transport routes, tourism, water sources and local climate.
exercises: Name two major physical features of Europe.
How have navigable rivers supported European development?
solutions: The Alps, North European Plain, Rhine, Danube, Scandinavian Peninsula and Mediterranean peninsulas are examples; any two are acceptable.
They provided transport routes, water, trade connections and sites for cities and industry.
practice_questions: Why is Europe's coastline useful for maritime connections?
Does Europe have one uniform culture or language?
practice_solutions: Its many seas, bays and peninsulas create numerous ports and relatively short routes to the sea.
No. Europe contains many countries, languages, histories and cultural traditions.
